name: Ryobi ONE+ 18V Hybrid WhisperSeries 7-1/2 in. Fan
summary: The best battery fan for most people, because ONE+ batteries are everywhere and the WhisperSeries is quiet enough to sleep beside.
verdict: Ryobi ONE+ is the battery platform most homeowners already have in the garage, and the WhisperSeries 7-1/2 inch fan is the most broadly useful fan on it. It slides onto any ONE+ 18V pack, and the hybrid design means it can also run from AC power when you are not in an outage, so it earns its shelf space year round. Ryobi tuned the WhisperSeries line for low noise, which matters more than airflow numbers when the fan is pointed at your pillow during a hot, powerless night. The blade is small, so think of it as a personal fan: one person at a desk, a sleeper, or a corner of a tent. Runtime depends entirely on the pack. By the capacity math, a 4Ah ONE+ battery stores about 72 watt-hours, which runs a small fan of this type for many hours on low. Owners of two or three packs can rotate them for days, especially with a way to recharge.

name: DEWALT 20V MAX Jobsite Fan
summary: The fan to buy if you are on DEWALT 20V MAX and want real airflow in a garage, attic or job site rather than a quiet bedside breeze.
verdict: The DEWALT 20V MAX Jobsite Fan is built for the conditions its name suggests: dusty, hot and hard on equipment. DEWALT lists an 11-inch blade, which pushes far more air than a desk-size fan and makes it useful for drying a freshly painted room, clearing fumes from a garage, or keeping a crew from cooking in an attic. The housing is designed to survive being knocked off a sawhorse, and the head pivots so you can aim it at a work area. More air means more power, so expect fewer hours per pack than from the Ryobi WhisperSeries at a similar speed. A 5Ah 20V MAX pack stores about 100 watt-hours by the capacity math, so a larger pack is the right companion for all-day use, and a second pack on the charger keeps it going. It is louder than the bedside fans here, which is fine for a job site and less fine for sleeping. For outages it doubles as a strong room fan.

name: Milwaukee M12 Compact Jobsite Fan
summary: A smart buy for M12 owners who work in tight spaces, but not the fan to cool a whole room.
verdict: Milwaukee's M12 line is popular with plumbers, electricians and HVAC techs because the packs are light and the tools are small, and the M12 Compact Jobsite Fan follows the same logic. It is small enough to wedge into a crawl space entrance, set on a ladder top or clip into a van, and it offers multiple speeds and an adjustable head so you can point it where you are working. The trade-off is the battery. M12 packs are 12-volt, so a 3Ah M12 battery holds about 36 watt-hours, roughly half what a similar amp-hour 18V pack stores. Expect respectable runtime on low and much shorter runtime on high. If you are already on M18 instead, Milwaukee also makes larger M18 fans worth comparing. For a homeowner without Milwaukee batteries, there is no reason to start a platform for this fan; one of the built-in-battery picks is simpler. For M12 owners, it is the obvious choice.

name: O2COOL Treva 10-Inch Portable Battery Fan
summary: The best fan for an emergency kit that may sit untouched for years, because a fresh pack of D cells is always ready when an outage hits.
verdict: The Treva line from O2COOL solves a problem rechargeable fans cannot: a lithium battery left on a shelf for two years may be flat, or worse, degraded, by the time you need it. The Treva 10-inch runs on D-cell batteries, which store a lot of energy for their price and keep most of their charge for years in a cool closet. That makes it the right fan for an emergency kit that lives in a basement until the next storm. D cells are also the battery most likely to still be on store shelves the day before a hurricane, after the lithium gear is gone. In normal use it can run from an AC adapter, so you are not burning batteries on ordinary summer days. The 10-inch blade is a step up from handheld fans and enough to keep one person comfortable at a bedside. Keep spare D cells with it, store the batteries out of the fan so they cannot leak into it, and rotate them every few years.

name: Geek Aire Rechargeable Outdoor Fan
summary: The pick for someone with no tool batteries who wants a real room fan that runs cordless for an evening or a night.
verdict: Geek Aire is one of the better-known brands making larger fans with a built-in rechargeable battery, closer to a floor or high-velocity fan than a desk accessory. That format is what most households without a tool platform actually want in an outage: something that charges from the wall while the power is on, then moves enough air to cool a bedroom or a patio for hours once it goes off. The lineup includes several sizes and battery capacities, and some models add a USB port for charging a phone, so read the specific listing for runtime, charge time and outputs before you buy. The trade-off with any built-in battery is that you cannot hot-swap a fresh pack. When it is empty, you need power to recharge it, which is where a small power station or solar panel comes in. For a family without Ryobi or DEWALT packs, it is a simpler, single-purchase answer than buying into a tool platform.

name: Jisulife Portable Handheld Fan
summary: A cheap, useful personal fan for commutes, events and outage nights, best bought in multiples and kept charged.
verdict: Jisulife is one of the most widely sold names in handheld rechargeable fans, and the appeal is obvious: a fan the size of a phone that charges over USB-C and fits in a pocket. In an outage it becomes a bedside fan that one person can point at their face while they fall asleep, and it recharges from the same power bank or power station that keeps your phone alive. During normal life it rides along to ballgames, theme parks and hot commutes. Be realistic about what it is. A handheld fan has a small internal battery and a small blade, so it moves air across one person at close range, and runtime on the highest speed is short compared with its low setting. Lineups and battery sizes change frequently, so check the specific model before buying, and favor ones that list battery capacity. Buy one per person in the household and they become the cheapest way to make a hot, powerless night bearable.

name: Lasko 3733 20-Inch Box Fan
summary: If you already own a power station, a plain 20-inch box fan is the most air per watt-hour you can buy for a summer outage.
verdict: This is not a battery fan, and that is the point. A 20-inch box fan moves a large volume of air with a simple motor, and box fans of this size commonly draw well under 100 watts even on high; check the label on yours for the exact figure. The Lasko 3733 is a typical three-speed model, sold in nearly every hardware store. Paired with a power station, it becomes a cordless room fan that outperforms every battery fan here on airflow. A 1kWh station running a box fan at around 60 watts would last in the range of 12 to 14 hours once inverter losses are counted, which covers a full night with plenty left for phones. Smaller stations work too; a 300Wh unit still runs one for several hours. The inefficiency is the inverter, which uses some power just to stay on, so a DC fan wins on small batteries. On a mid-size or larger station, though, the box fan is the best value cooling you can buy.
